topics.label: Rebirth
topics.intro: Does anything carry on after death, and if so, what? The Buddha said a stream of becoming continues without a fixed self. The Upanishads said the Self is untouched while the subtle body moves on. Plato told the Myth of Er. Theosophy and Steiner rebuilt the idea for the modern West. Start anywhere and keep going.

takes.Theravāda: Craving and kamma drive a new birth, yet no unchanging self passes from life to life.
takes.Tibetan Buddhism: Between death and the next birth lies the bardo, where the mind meets its own nature and its habits.
takes.Vedānta: The subtle body moves from life to life, carried by karma; the Self you are was never born and never dies.
takes.Platonic tradition: The soul is immortal and returns to new lives, choosing its next life by what it has become (the Myth of Er).
takes.Anthroposophy: The human I returns through repeated earth lives, meeting the karma it has made and growing through it.
takes.Krishnamurti: Asks what it is that would be reborn: the stream of memory called the self can end now, which matters more than a next life.

topics.label: Karma
topics.intro: Karma is intention, said the Buddha. The Gita says act, and let go of the fruit. The West rebuilt it as moral law and destiny.

takes.Theravāda: Kamma is intention: what you will and do shapes what you meet and who you become.
takes.Tibetan Buddhism: Actions ripen across lives; purification and merit change how they ripen, and wisdom uproots them.
takes.Vedānta: Action binds as long as it is done for its fruits; action offered without attachment frees.
takes.Kashmir Shaivism: Karma is one of the three impurities that veil consciousness; recognising your nature as Śiva dissolves it.
takes.Kriya Yoga: Right action and meditation work out past karma; Kriya practice is taught as a way to hasten it.
takes.Anthroposophy: Karma is a just weaving of destiny across lives, worked out in the meetings and trials of each new life.
takes.The Fourth Way: Most of what we call action is mechanical; only conscious effort is truly ours.

topics.label: Self & not-self
topics.intro: Who am I? The Buddha said: not this, not this, not this. The Upanishads said: that thou art. Ramana said: ask, and find out.

takes.Theravāda: Nothing you can point to as yours is a lasting self; seeing this ends the conceit 'I am'.
takes.Zen: Study the self to forget the self: the self, like all things, has no fixed essence apart from everything else.
takes.Tibetan Buddhism: The self is empty of inherent existence; it exists only as a label placed on body and mind.
takes.Vedānta: Ask 'Who am I?': under every thought is the one Self, pure awareness, which is Brahman.
takes.Kashmir Shaivism: The self is Śiva, free consciousness; awakening is recognising what you already are.
takes.Christian mysticism: Let go of the self that clings, and God is found in the ground of the soul.
takes.The Fourth Way: We have no single permanent I, only many passing 'I's; a real I has to be built through work on oneself.
takes.Krishnamurti: The self is a bundle of memory and reaction; to see it clearly, without a watcher, is freedom.

topics.label: Emptiness
topics.intro: Form is emptiness, emptiness is form. For the Madhyamaka, nothing exists from its own side; for Zen, emptiness is this very moment; for Thich Nhat Hanh, it is interbeing; for Dzogchen, it is the open ground of mind. Here the Buddhist schools, and a few outside them, explain what emptiness is and is not.

topics.label: Meditation
topics.intro: Breath, mantra, koan, prayer, open awareness. The same question asked in many ways: how do we come home?

takes.Theravāda: Restraint and right view first; then the mind settles and sees the arising and passing of things.
takes.Zen: Just sit: practice is not a means to awakening but its expression.
takes.Tibetan Buddhism: Calm the mind, then recognise its nature: awareness itself, open and clear.
takes.Vedānta: Quiet the mind through discipline or devotion, then rest as the awareness in which all experience comes and goes.
takes.Kashmir Shaivism: Practices such as those of the Vijñāna Bhairava turn any moment of experience back to the consciousness it arises in.
takes.Kriya Yoga: Breath and life-energy techniques still the mind and turn it inward, toward the divine.
takes.Christian mysticism: Contemplative prayer: rest in God beyond words and images.
takes.The Fourth Way: Self-remembering: be present to yourself in the middle of ordinary life.
takes.Krishnamurti: Not a method but choiceless awareness: watching the movement of thought without a controller.

topics.label: Kundalini & the subtle body
topics.intro: The subtle body: channels, centres and a coiled power at the base of the spine. Haṭha yoga, the tantras of Kashmir and the Goddess, Tibetan yogas and modern teachers describe it differently, and scholars trace where the idea came from. Here are the teachers, the history, and the cautions.

takes.Theravāda: Life as we grasp it is unsatisfying; see its cause and it can end.
takes.Zen: Suffering is met, not escaped: held in mindful attention, it can be transformed.
takes.Tibetan Buddhism: Suffering comes from grasping at a self; seeing others suffer as we do is the root of compassion.
takes.Vedānta: Suffering comes from taking yourself to be the body and mind.
takes.Christian traditions: Suffering can be carried and transformed, in communion with Christ's own.
takes.Krishnamurti: Sorrow ends when you meet it completely, without escaping into explanation.

takes.Theravāda: Craving is the origin of suffering; when it fades, suffering ends.
takes.Zen: Desire is met with open attention rather than fought; seen as empty, it loosens by itself.
takes.Vedānta: Desire for the fruits of action keeps the wheel turning; the longing for liberation is the one desire worth keeping.
takes.Platonic tradition: Desire is redirected, not destroyed: love rises from beautiful things toward Beauty itself.
takes.Christian mysticism: Detachment: want nothing but God, and the soul is free.

topics.label: Death
topics.intro: Every tradition starts here. Remember death, the Buddha said, with every breath. The Stoics and Socrates practised it. The Tibetans mapped it. Ramana enacted it at sixteen.

takes.Theravāda: Recollect death daily: it loosens clinging and shows the urgency of the path.
takes.Zen: Birth and death are the life of the way itself; seen clearly, they lose their grip on the mind.
takes.Tibetan Buddhism: Death is a doorway: rightly prepared, the moment of dying can be the moment of liberation.
takes.Vedānta: Death belongs to the body and the mind; find out who it is that fears it.
takes.Platonic tradition: Philosophy is practice for dying: the soul's training in turning from the body toward what is real.
takes.Anthroposophy: After death the soul looks back on its life, is purified (kamaloca) and prepares for a new birth.
takes.Krishnamurti: Die each day to what you know and hold; then death is not at the far end of life but within it.

topics.label: Awakening
topics.intro: Nibbāna, moksha, satori, gnosis, the unitive life. What is it, and how does anyone arrive?

takes.Theravāda: Nibbāna is the ending of greed, hatred and delusion, reached through stages that cannot be lost.
takes.Zen: Awakening is seeing your own nature, sudden or gradual, and then living it.
takes.Tibetan Buddhism: Buddhahood is the full recognition of the mind's own nature, wisdom and compassion inseparable.
takes.Vedānta: Liberation is not gained; it is the end of the mistaken belief that you were ever bound.
takes.Kashmir Shaivism: Liberation is recognition (pratyabhijñā): you have always been Śiva, free consciousness.
takes.Neoplatonism: The soul turns inward and ascends until it is one with the One.
takes.Christian mysticism: Union with God, reached through love and letting go, in which the soul finds God in its own ground.
takes.The Fourth Way: We are asleep; waking up begins with seeing our own mechanicalness and remembering ourselves.

topics.label: Faith & devotion
topics.intro: Devotion is the path of the heart: love turned toward the divine, a teacher, or a name. Bhakti sings it, Pure Land entrusts itself to Amida, the Sufi remembers God with every breath, the Christian prays without ceasing. Here the traditions describe what surrender is, and how it is practised.

topics.label: Reality & illusion
topics.intro: Not two. Advaita says the world is Brahman appearing as many; Kashmir Shaivism says it is consciousness recognising itself; Dzogchen and Zen point to a nature that was never divided; the philosophers of the sacred ask whether mind comes first. Here is nonduality, and the question of what is real.
questions: Māyā: is the world an illusion?

topics.label: The imaginal
topics.intro: Between the world of the senses and the world of pure ideas lies a third: the imaginal, Henry Corbin's word for the realm where visions, angels and archetypes are real. Sufis, Renaissance Platonists, Jung and Hillman, and today's scholars of myth and cosmology explore it. Here is imagination taken seriously.

practices.name: The five remembrances
cautions: Reflections on death can stir grief. Go gently, and set the practice aside if it overwhelms you.
practices.summary: Each day, recollect slowly: I am subject to ageing; to illness; to death; I will be parted from all that is dear; I am the owner of my actions, and will inherit them. Let each one sink in before the next.

practices.name: Mindfulness of death (maranasati)
cautions: Reflections on death can stir grief. Go gently, and set the practice aside if it overwhelms you.
practices.summary: At nightfall and daybreak, reflect that death could come tonight or today from many causes, and ask whether any unskilful quality is still unabandoned. Let the urgency feed effort, not fear.

practices.name: Recollecting the round
cautions: Keep the breath natural and unforced. Stop if you feel dizzy, anxious or unwell.
Reflections on death can stir grief. Go gently, and set the practice aside if it overwhelms you.
practices.summary: Contemplate how long the round of birth and death has been, and how many losses it holds, until disenchantment with becoming arises. Then turn to the breath and rest.

practices.name: Powa: an introduction to transference at death
cautions: Orientation only: this practice is traditionally learned from a qualified teacher in its lineage. Read and listen; do not attempt it from a summary.
Reflections on death can stir grief. Go gently, and set the practice aside if it overwhelms you.
practices.summary: Read a traditional introduction before seeking instruction from a qualified teacher: refuge, visualising Amitabha above the crown, and training the mind's direction at death. It is taught with empowerment, not from a page.

practices.name: Preparing for the bardo
cautions: Reflections on death can stir grief. Go gently, and set the practice aside if it overwhelms you.
practices.summary: Notice the small gaps of daily life (falling asleep, the pause between thoughts) as rehearsals for the great transition, and rest there as awareness.
practices.sourceLabel: Lion's Roar: The Fine Art of Conscious Dying (Glenn Mullin)

practices.name: Self-enquiry: who dies?
cautions: Reflections on death can stir grief. Go gently, and set the practice aside if it overwhelms you.
practices.summary: When the thought of death comes, ask to whom it comes. Trace the 'I' back to its source instead of following the thought. Ramana's own awakening began by lying down and enacting his death.
practices.sourceLabel: Who Am I? (Sri Ramanasramam, free PDF)

practices.name: Practising dying (melete thanatou)
cautions: Reflections on death can stir grief. Go gently, and set the practice aside if it overwhelms you.
practices.summary: Socrates calls philosophy the practice of dying: loosening the soul's grip on the body's pleasures and fears, day by day. Read the Phaedo slowly as an exercise, not an argument.

practices.name: Powa: an introduction
cautions: Orientation only: this practice is traditionally learned from a qualified teacher in its lineage. Read and listen; do not attempt it from a summary.
Reflections on death can stir grief. Go gently, and set the practice aside if it overwhelms you.

practices.name: Analytic meditation on the stages of the path
cautions: Reflections on death can stir grief. Go gently, and set the practice aside if it overwhelms you.
practices.summary: Pick one Lamrim topic, such as the preciousness of this human life or the certainty of death. Think it through step by step, using reasons and examples, until a felt conviction comes. Then rest single-pointedly on that conviction for a while. Alternate thinking and resting.

practices.name: Self-enquiry
practices.summary: Whenever a thought arises, ask to whom it arises; the answer is 'to me'; then ask 'who am I?' and hold attention on the sense of I.

practices.name: Contemplating not-self
practices.summary: Take each aggregate in turn and ask: is it constant, is it easeful, is it fitting to regard it as me, mine, my self?

practices.name: Shiva Process self-inquiry
practices.summary: Bring to mind a situation that is troubling you. Describe what you feel in plain words, then ask "what is the deeper feeling under this?" and keep going, layer by layer, until something shifts and the contraction releases. Often done in pairs or with a guide.

practices.name: "What am I? Don't know"
cautions: Keep the breath natural and unforced. Stop if you feel dizzy, anxious or unwell.
practices.summary: Ask "What am I?" deeply on the in-breath. On the out-breath, hold "Don't know..." as long as the breath lasts. Return to this don't-know mind in every activity, and keep clear about the next correct action. This is Seung Sahn's Kwan Um teaching.

practices.name: Owner of my actions
practices.summary: The fifth remembrance: I am the owner of my actions, heir to my actions. Recollect it before acting and after.

practices.name: Mindfulness of breathing
cautions: Keep the breath natural and unforced. Stop if you feel dizzy, anxious or unwell.
practices.summary: Sit comfortably, know the in-breath and out-breath, then let the breath calm the whole body before turning to feelings and mind.

practices.name: Goodwill (metta)
practices.summary: Wish yourself well, then widen the wish to others, near and far, seen and unseen, without exception.

practices.name: Resting in the gap between breaths (Vijñāna Bhairava dhāraṇā)
cautions: Keep the breath natural and unforced. Stop if you feel dizzy, anxious or unwell.
practices.summary: Sit comfortably and breathe naturally. Notice the instant where the in-breath turns into the out-breath, and the instant where the out-breath turns back. Do not hold the breath; simply let attention fall into each turning point and rest there for its brief duration. Over time, notice the open awareness that is present in the pause.
practices.sourceLabel: Bettina Bäumer, Vijñāna Bhairava verses 24–27 (the breath dhāraṇās).

practices.name: Recognition (pratyabhijñā) contemplation
practices.summary: Read one sūtra of the Pratyabhijñāhṛdayam slowly. Then look at present experience — a sound, a thought, a feeling — and ask whether anything appears outside awareness. Let the understanding "this too is a form of the one consciousness" settle as a felt recognition rather than an idea. Return to the text, then to experience, alternating.
practices.sourceLabel: Christopher Wallis on the twenty sūtras of the Pratyabhijñāhṛdayam.

practices.name: Drawing the Śrī Chakra as meditation
practices.summary: Following a teacher's step-by-step construction, draw the Śrī Yantra slowly from the centre point (bindu) outward: the nine interlocking triangles, the lotus rings and the square gateways. Treat each stage as a contemplation of the goddess unfolding into the world, not as geometry homework.
practices.sourceLabel: Devipuram, "How to Draw Sri Chakra" parts 1–2.

practices.name: Basic Śaiva Siddhānta meditation
cautions: Keep the breath natural and unforced. Stop if you feel dizzy, anxious or unwell.
practices.summary: Sit upright, regulate the breath to a slow even count, then draw awareness inward from the senses to the spine and to the inner light, holding a single point of focus. Hinduism Today's monastery teaches it as part of daily worship and study.
practices.sourceLabel: Bodhinatha Veylanswami, "How Do We Meditate? Part 1".

practices.name: Mantra repetition (japa)
practices.summary: Choose a mantra received from your tradition, sit with a mala, and repeat it at an even pace, aloud, whispered or mentally. Let attention rest on the sound and its meaning; when the mind wanders, return to the next repetition.

practices.name: Ānāpānasati (breath meditation, "Method 2")
practices.tradition: Dhammayut forest line (Ajahn Mun → Maha Boowa / Ajaan Lee)
cautions: Keep the breath natural and unforced. Stop if you feel dizzy, anxious or unwell.
practices.summary: Sit upright and notice the breath at whatever point it is clearest. Let it settle into a comfortable rhythm, then let that sense of ease spread through the whole body, using the breath energy as a home base for steady, alert attention.

practices.name: "Buddho" recollection
cautions: Keep the breath natural and unforced. Stop if you feel dizzy, anxious or unwell.
practices.summary: Silently repeat "bud-" on the in-breath and "-dho" on the out-breath to anchor the mind; when the mind is calm, drop the word and stay with the knowing itself. Used widely in the Ajahn Mun and Ajahn Chah lines.

practices.name: Walking meditation (jongrom)
practices.tradition: Ajahn Chah line (Wat Nong Pah Pong)
practices.summary: Choose a straight path of 15–30 paces. Walk at a natural or slow pace, attention on the feet or the whole body; at each end, stop, turn, and re-collect before walking back.

practices.name: Mahasi noting
practices.summary: Watch the rise and fall of the abdomen and give each event a soft mental label ("rising", "falling", "thinking", "hearing"), then return to the primary object; move to slow walking with labels for lifting, moving and placing.

practices.name: Natural awareness (right attitude)
practices.summary: Instead of forcing focus on one object, relax and know whatever is being experienced, checking the attitude of the observing mind (craving, aversion, impatience) throughout daily activities.

practices.name: Satipaṭṭhāna (four establishings of mindfulness)
practices.summary: Contemplate body, feeling, mind and mental qualities as they arise and pass, ardent, clearly knowing and mindful, without greed or distress about the world (MN 10).

practices.name: RAIN
practices.summary: Recognise what is happening; Allow it to be there; Investigate with kindness how it feels in the body; Nurture with self-compassion; then rest in the awareness that remains.

practices.name: Open awareness (shamatha without a support)
practices.summary: After a few minutes with a support, let it go. Leave the eyes open and the gaze soft. Let sights, sounds and thoughts come and go, and do not follow them or push them away. When you get caught up, simply notice it and relax again. The point is to rest as the knowing that is already present.

practices.name: Looking at the mind (Mahamudra)
practices.summary: Once the mind is calm, turn and look for the one who is looking. Ask where a thought comes from, where it stays, and where it goes. Do not reason about it; just look and rest in whatever is seen or not found. This practice is traditionally done under a qualified teacher's guidance.

practices.name: Resting in rigpa (Dzogchen), orientation only
cautions: Orientation only: this practice is traditionally learned from a qualified teacher in its lineage. Read and listen; do not attempt it from a summary.
practices.summary: In Dzogchen, the student is introduced to the nature of mind (rigpa) by a teacher. Between sessions, practitioners recall that recognition, leave it uncontrived for short moments, many times, and release any effort to improve it. This entry describes the practice and is not a substitute for the introduction itself.

practices.name: Shikantaza (just sitting)
practices.summary: Sit as in zazen, but drop counting and any object. Simply sit, aware of the whole posture and the whole field of experience, without chasing or suppressing anything. When you find yourself lost in thought, come back to the posture. Dogen treats the sitting itself as realisation, not as a means to it.

practices.name: Koan practice with Mu
cautions: Keep the breath natural and unforced. Stop if you feel dizzy, anxious or unwell.
practices.summary: Take up "Does a dog have buddha nature? Mu" (Zhaozhou). Breathe Mu on each exhalation and put your whole doubt into it. Do not interpret it. Present your understanding to a teacher in private interview (dokusan). Koan work depends on that meeting with a teacher.

practices.name: Silent illumination (mozhao)
practices.summary: Relax the body and be aware of the whole body sitting. Widen that awareness to include the environment, without any centre or edge. Silence means not adding commentary; illumination means remaining clearly aware. Rest there, and return whenever you get caught.

practices.name: Bhairavi Sadhana (Isha)
cautions: Orientation only: this practice is traditionally learned from a qualified teacher in its lineage. Read and listen; do not attempt it from a summary.
practices.summary: A lay devotional observance offered by the Isha Foundation around Linga Bhairavi: for a set period the practitioner keeps simple disciplines (as given by Isha), offers daily devotion to the goddess, and completes it with an offering at a Linga Bhairavi abode. The exact rules come from the organisation each year.

practices.name: Śravaṇa–manana–nididhyāsana
practices.summary: Systematic listening to the Upaniṣads with a teacher (śravaṇa), resolving doubts by reflection (manana), and dwelling on the understood meaning until it is assimilated (nididhyāsana).

practices.name: Japa (repetition of a divine name)
practices.summary: Repeat a mantra or name of God given by the teacher, often with a mālā of 108 beads, letting the mind rest in its meaning and the feeling of devotion.

practices.name: Hare Krishna mahāmantra (japa and kīrtan)
practices.summary: Chant "Hare Kṛṣṇa Hare Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa Kṛṣṇa Hare Hare / Hare Rāma Hare Rāma, Rāma Rāma Hare Hare" softly on beads (japa) or sing it together (kīrtan), as practised since Chaitanya.

practices.name: Nembutsu / nianfo
practices.summary: Recite "Namu Amida Butsu" (Japanese) or "Namo Amituofo" (Chinese), aloud or silently, with a mala if you like. In Chinese Pure Land, recitation is a practice of concentration and aspiration for rebirth. In Shin Buddhism, it is an expression of gratitude for Amida's vow, not a means of earning anything.

practices.name: Christian meditation with a mantra (Maranatha)
practices.summary: Sit still and upright with your eyes lightly closed. Silently repeat one prayer-word, "Ma-ra-na-tha", in four equal syllables, listening to it rather than thinking about its meaning. When thoughts or images arrive, return to the word, without force. Sit for 20–30 minutes, morning and evening.

practices.name: Centering Prayer
practices.summary: Choose a sacred word as a sign of consent to God's presence. Sit comfortably and bring it in gently. When you notice you are engaged with a thought, return ever so gently to the word. End by resting in silence for a couple of minutes. Twice daily, 20 minutes.

practices.name: Lectio Divina
practices.summary: Read a short scripture passage slowly, then again; notice the word that catches you; respond to it in prayer; rest in silence. Read, ponder, pray, rest.

practices.name: The Jesus Prayer (prayer of the heart)
practices.summary: Repeat "Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me" slowly and attentively, often with a prayer rope, keeping the mind in the words and letting it descend into the heart. Begin with a fixed time each day; humility and stillness come before technique.

practices.name: Zikr (remembrance) in the Inayati way
cautions: Keep the breath natural and unforced. Stop if you feel dizzy, anxious or unwell.
practices.summary: Sitting quietly, repeat the phrase of divine unity (La ilaha illa'llah) aloud or silently, letting the breath and a gentle movement of the head carry it, until the remembrance continues on its own in the heart.

practices.name: Dhikr and breathwork
cautions: Keep the breath natural and unforced. Stop if you feel dizzy, anxious or unwell.
practices.summary: Join a short divine name or phrase to the in- and out-breath; keep attention on the heart; finish with silence and a prayer.

practices.name: Khatm-i Khwajagan (Naqshbandi group dhikr)
practices.summary: A set Naqshbandi litany of Qur'an recitation, blessings on the Prophet and silent or vocal remembrance, recited together under a shaykh's guidance.

practices.name: Weekly parashah reflection (neo-Hasidic)
practices.summary: Each week read the Torah portion with a Hasidic commentary in mind and look for the inward, devotional teaching it holds for this week of your life.

practices.name: Calming and contemplation (zhiguan)
cautions: Keep the breath natural and unforced. Stop if you feel dizzy, anxious or unwell.
practices.summary: First calm the mind (zhi) by settling the breath and posture. Then contemplate (guan) any present thought as simultaneously empty, provisionally existing, and the middle, which are the threefold truth. Zhiyi's Mohe zhiguan sets out four kinds of samadhi practice (constant sitting, constant walking, half-walking half-sitting, and neither).

practices.name: Rudi's double breath
cautions: Orientation only: this practice is traditionally learned from a qualified teacher in its lineage. Read and listen; do not attempt it from a summary.
practices.summary: Breathe in, bringing attention down from the throat into the heart, and then down to the navel and the base of the body. Breathing out, let the energy rise up the spine. Keep the movement gentle and continuous, and return to the heart when attention scatters.
practices.sourceLabel: Swami Khecaranatha on Rudi's double breath.

practices.name: Khecarī mudrā (historical description only)
cautions: Orientation only: this practice is traditionally learned from a qualified teacher in its lineage. Read and listen; do not attempt it from a summary.
practices.summary: Described in haṭha texts as turning the tongue back and up into the cavity above the soft palate, sometimes after gradually lengthening the tongue. We list it for context: the full form involves cutting the frenum and is not something to try from a video.
practices.sourceLabel: Mallinson, The Khecarīvidyā (DPhil); no short clip on file.

practices.name: Dream yoga, first steps
practices.summary: During the day, keep reminding yourself "this is a dream" so that the habit carries into sleep. Before sleep, set a strong intention to recognise dreams. Visualise a luminous syllable at the throat as you fall asleep. Each morning, review whether you recognised a dream, and renew the intention.

practices.name: Feeding your demons (a modern adaptation of Chöd)
practices.summary: Find a struggle, such as fear or a craving, and feel where it lives in the body. Picture it as a figure in front of you and ask what it wants and what it really needs. Then imagine dissolving your body into nectar that gives it exactly that, until it is satisfied. Rest in the open space that remains.

practices.name: The view from above (spiritual exercise)
practices.summary: In imagination, rise above your situation until your concerns appear in the scale of the cosmos; return with a lighter, more just sense of what matters. One of the ancient "spiritual exercises" Pierre Hadot described.

practices.name: Hermetic ascent and rebirth (Corpus Hermeticum XIII)
practices.summary: Read slowly and as contemplation, not just as information: the treatise guides the reader to put away the "torments" of matter and be reborn as the intellect praising God in silence.

practices.name: Active imagination / imaginal attention
practices.summary: Stay with an image (from a dream, a text or a place) as a living presence; let it speak and move; respond to it honestly rather than interpreting it away. In Corbin's terms it is a perception of the mundus imaginalis.

practices.name: Neelakantha Meditation (mantra-based)
practices.summary: This is an initiated mantra practice: the mantra is received from an authorised teacher. In outline, one sits twice a day, repeats the given mantra inwardly and lets it become subtle, treating the body as a stable platform rather than an obstacle. Learn it from the school; we describe it only so users know what the clips refer to.

practices.name: Nyāsa — placing mantra on the body
practices.summary: Touch or attend to specific points of the body (heart, head, crown, arms) while silently repeating the syllables assigned to them, so the body is treated as a seat of the deity before worship or meditation. Traditionally learnt with the specific mantra from a teacher.
practices.sourceLabel: Sthaneshwar Timalsina, "What is Nyasa and why do we do it?"

practices.name: Contemplating the Twelve Kālīs (Krama)
practices.summary: Take one Kālī of the Krama sequence at a time (e.g. Sṛṣṭikālī, the Kālī of creation). Study what phase of cognition she stands for — an object arising, being held, being withdrawn into the knower — and watch that phase in your own experience during the day.
practices.sourceLabel: Yamajit, Twelve Kālīs of the Krama lineage, part I.

practices.name: Mettā (loving-kindness)
practices.summary: Wish well to yourself, then a benefactor, a friend, a neutral person, a difficult person and finally all beings, using simple phrases or a felt sense of goodwill, letting it spread in every direction.

practices.name: Body sweeping (Goenka vipassanā)
practices.summary: After a few days of ānāpāna to sharpen attention, move attention systematically through the body from head to feet, observing every sensation with equanimity, as taught in ten-day residential courses.

practices.name: Yoga nidrā
cautions: Keep the breath natural and unforced. Stop if you feel dizzy, anxious or unwell.
practices.summary: Lying down, rotate awareness through the body, then breath, opposite sensations and visualisations while staying awake, ending with a personal resolve (saṅkalpa).

practices.name: Five points of yoga (Sivananda)
cautions: Keep the breath natural and unforced. Stop if you feel dizzy, anxious or unwell.
Reflections on death can stir grief. Go gently, and set the practice aside if it overwhelms you.
practices.summary: Proper exercise (āsana), proper breathing (prāṇāyāma), proper relaxation, proper diet and positive thinking with meditation, as summarised by Swami Vishnudevananda.

practices.name: Breath-centred, individually adapted āsana (viniyoga)
cautions: Keep the breath natural and unforced. Stop if you feel dizzy, anxious or unwell.
practices.summary: Link every movement to a slow inhale or exhale and adapt sequence, length and intensity to the person's body, age and aims, as taught by Krishnamacharya and T. K. V. Desikachar.

practices.name: Calm abiding with a support
cautions: Keep the breath natural and unforced. Stop if you feel dizzy, anxious or unwell.
practices.summary: Sit upright and relaxed. Rest your attention lightly on a simple support, such as the breath at the nostrils, a pebble, or a sound. When you notice the mind has wandered, return to the support without scolding yourself. Aim for many short, clear sessions rather than a few long, dull ones. Over time, loosen your grip until attention rests on its own.

practices.name: Tonglen (sending and taking)
cautions: Keep the breath natural and unforced. Stop if you feel dizzy, anxious or unwell.
practices.summary: Flash briefly on open, spacious mind. Then breathe in a feeling of heaviness and heat, and breathe out a feeling of coolness and light. Start with a real person who is suffering, perhaps yourself, and breathe in their pain while breathing out relief. Widen this to everyone who feels the same. Keep it simple and close to how you actually feel.

practices.name: Mind training (lojong) slogans
practices.summary: Choose one of the 59 slogans of Atisha's Seven Points, such as "Drive all blames into one". Carry it through the day. When irritation or self-cherishing comes up, recall the slogan and look again at the situation. Review the day each evening.

practices.name: Nine breathings of purification
cautions: Keep the breath natural and unforced. Stop if you feel dizzy, anxious or unwell.
practices.summary: Visualise the three channels: a central blue channel with a white one on the right and a red one on the left. Breathe in through the right nostril and out through the left three times, releasing anger. Then breathe in through the left and out through the right three times, releasing attachment. Finally, breathe in through both and push the breath up the central channel three times, releasing ignor

practices.name: Zazen posture and breath
cautions: Keep the breath natural and unforced. Stop if you feel dizzy, anxious or unwell.
practices.summary: Sit on a cushion with your knees on the floor, or on a chair, with the spine upright. Rest the hands in the cosmic mudra, left on right with the thumbs lightly touching, and keep the eyes half-open and lowered. Breathe naturally through the nose. Beginners can count breaths from one to ten and start again whenever they lose count.

practices.name: Huatou (critical phrase)
practices.summary: Take up a short question, such as "What is wu?" or "Before my parents were born, what was my original face?" Keep asking it with a sense of genuine not-knowing until a "great doubt" gathers. Return to the question whenever you lose it. This is Sheng Yen's method, best done in retreat with guidance.

practices.name: Mindful breathing with gathas
cautions: Keep the breath natural and unforced. Stop if you feel dizzy, anxious or unwell.
practices.summary: Breathe in and silently say "In"; breathe out and say "Out". As you settle, shorten it to "Deep / Slow", "Calm / Ease" or "Smile / Release". Use a bell or a phone chime as a reminder to stop, breathe three times and come back to the body.

practices.name: Walking meditation
cautions: Keep the breath natural and unforced. Stop if you feel dizzy, anxious or unwell.
practices.summary: Walk slowly and coordinate your steps with your breath, for example two steps on the in-breath and three on the out-breath. Feel each foot touching the earth as if kissing it. You are not trying to arrive anywhere; every step is the arrival.

practices.name: Ajikan (A-syllable meditation)
cautions: Orientation only: this practice is traditionally learned from a qualified teacher in its lineage. Read and listen; do not attempt it from a summary.
practices.summary: Shingon practitioners visualise the Sanskrit syllable A on a moon disc above a lotus. The A signifies the unborn source of all things. They join it with the breath and expand the moon until it fills the universe, then contract it into the heart. Formal ajikan is taught after initiation; this entry is an orientation only.

practices.name: Video lectio (short contemplative reading)
practices.summary: Watch a short image or text slowly, then sit with a single phrase that stays with you before meditating.

practices.name: Welcoming Practice
practices.summary: When a strong reaction arises, feel it as a sensation in the body; say "welcome" to it instead of resisting; then let go of the desire for security, approval or control, and so release it into presence.

practices.name: Neoplatonic contemplation ("strip away everything")
practices.summary: Following Plotinus, turn attention from objects to the activity of knowing, then let even that subtle self-image fall away, resting in the simple presence it comes from. Usually practised after a period of calming meditation.

practices.name: Letter-combination meditation (ecstatic Kabbalah)
cautions: Keep the breath natural and unforced. Stop if you feel dizzy, anxious or unwell.
practices.summary: Abulafia's path: combine and permute the Hebrew letters of divine names, with breath and pronunciation, to loosen ordinary thinking. Historically taught only under a teacher. Listed here for context, not as instruction.

practices.name: The Middle Pillar (outline)
practices.tradition: Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn
cautions: Energy visualisation: stop if you feel agitated, pressured in the head or chest, or unwell.
Psychologically intense imagery; set aside if it overwhelms you.
Orientation only: this practice is traditionally learned from a qualified teacher in its lineage. Read and listen; do not attempt it from a summary.
practices.summary: Stand or sit straight. Picture a slender pillar of light along the midline of the body. Bring attention to five centers in turn, seeing each as a sphere of its colour: brilliant white above the crown; soft lavender at the throat; rose pink at the heart; deep violet at the loins; and at the feet the four earth tones quartered. Dwell briefly at each. Then picture light circulating: down the front of
practices.sourceLabel: Regardie, The Middle Pillar (1938). Centres, colours and circulation as published; vibratory formulae omitted. Wikipedia link checked 200 on 2026-10-20.

practices.name: Ease through the body with the breath (Trika prep)
cautions: Keep the breath natural; never hold it or force it.
If you feel disoriented, unreal or anxious, open the eyes, feel the feet and the seat, and stop for today.
This week is a foundation only. Initiated Trika practice (mantra, breath retention, subtle-body work) is learned from a qualified teacher in the tradition.
Keep the breath natural and unforced. Stop if you feel dizzy, anxious or unwell.
practices.summary: Sit upright and let the breath settle into a comfortable rhythm. Notice where the breath is clearest and rest attention there. Let that sense of ease spread through the whole body, using the breath as a home base for steady attention. When the mind wanders, return gently to the breath without force. Close by sitting quietly for a few breaths and noticing the whole body at once.
practices.sourceLabel: Thanissaro Bhikkhu breath method (free, publisher site); used here as the Trika-prep foundation for steady attention before gap and recognition work.

practices.name: Listening to the inner sound (VBT verses 38-39)
cautions: If you live with tinnitus that distresses you, listen instead to an outer sound such as a bell or a held note as it fades (verses 40-41).
If you feel disoriented, unreal or anxious, open the eyes, feel the feet and the seat, and stop for today.
The rest of the Vijñāna Bhairava (breath retention, mantra, the subtle-body and burning practices) is learned from a qualified teacher in the Trika tradition; Satsang lists places to practise.
Keep the breath natural and unforced. Stop if you feel dizzy, anxious or unwell.
practices.summary: Sit comfortably and let the breath settle by itself. Listen for a faint inner sound, a soft ringing or hum beneath the sounds of the room. Rest attention on it lightly, without straining to hear. Let it be loud, soft, present or absent; do not follow it into images or stories. When the mind wanders, come back to listening. If the sound fades into quiet, rest in the quiet. When you finish, notice t
practices.sourceLabel: Vijñāna Bhairava verses 38-39 (nāda-yoga), tr. Christopher Hareesh Wallis (Tantra 112 full text) and his blog post on these verses. Satsang summary in its own words.

practices.name: The body as awareness (VBT verse 63)
cautions: If you feel disoriented, unreal or anxious, open the eyes, feel the feet and the seat, and stop for today.
If you have a history of trauma, dissociation, psychosis or severe anxiety, keep sits short with eyes open, or practise with a qualified teacher or clinician.
The rest of the Vijñāna Bhairava (breath retention, mantra, the subtle-body and burning practices) is learned from a qualified teacher in the Trika tradition; Satsang lists places to practise.
practices.summary: Sit and let attention rest on the whole body at once: not one part, the whole field of sensation. Then take the body, and the world around it, as made of awareness. Let this be felt rather than thought. When the mind narrows back to "me" and "mine", return to the wider field and rest there. The body stays where it is; only the sense of it being separate softens.
practices.sourceLabel: Vijñāna Bhairava verse 63, tr. Christopher Hareesh Wallis (Tantra 112 full text). Satsang summary in its own words.

practices.name: Resting between objects (VBT verse 62)
cautions: If you feel disoriented, unreal or anxious, open the eyes, feel the feet and the seat, and stop for today.
The rest of the Vijñāna Bhairava (breath retention, mantra, the subtle-body and burning practices) is learned from a qualified teacher in the Trika tradition; Satsang lists places to practise.
Keep the breath natural and unforced. Stop if you feel dizzy, anxious or unwell.
practices.summary: First settle with the breath for a few minutes. Then notice the moment the mind lets go of one thing, a sensation, a thought, a sound, and before it takes up the next. Rest in that in-between. Do not chase the next object and do not push it away. When you find you have already moved on, come back to the gap. Practise the breath-pause sit first; this one needs a little steadiness.
practices.sourceLabel: Vijñāna Bhairava verse 62 (with 61), tr. Christopher Hareesh Wallis (Tantra 112 full text). Satsang summary in its own words.

practices.name: Spaciousness: a wall of skin with nothing inside (VBT verses 43-48)
cautions: If you feel disoriented, unreal or anxious, open the eyes, feel the feet and the seat, and stop for today.
If you have a history of trauma, dissociation, psychosis or severe anxiety, keep sits short with eyes open, or practise with a qualified teacher or clinician.
The rest of the Vijñāna Bhairava (breath retention, mantra, the subtle-body and burning practices) is learned from a qualified teacher in the Trika tradition; Satsang lists places to practise.
practices.summary: Sit and notice the space of the room around you, the space that holds the walls and your body. Then sense the space inside the body: the chest, the mouth, the skull. Feel the skin as a thin wall with open space within and without. Let the inner and outer space be one field and rest in that openness. When the mind reaches for something solid, notice the reaching and return to space. Stay alert; thi
practices.sourceLabel: Vijñāna Bhairava verses 43-48 (the spaciousness practices; verse 48: the skin as a wall with nothing inside), tr. Christopher Hareesh Wallis (Tantra 112 full text) and his blog post on these verses. Satsang summary in its own words.

practices.name: Touching the end-of-twelve through the day (VBT verse 51)
cautions: If attention above the head brings headache, pressure or dizziness, rest it in the heart or the soles of the feet instead.
If you feel disoriented, unreal or anxious, open the eyes, feel the feet and the seat, and stop for today.
The rest of the Vijñāna Bhairava (breath retention, mantra, the subtle-body and burning practices) is learned from a qualified teacher in the Trika tradition; Satsang lists places to practise.
Keep the breath natural and unforced. Stop if you feel dizzy, anxious or unwell.
practices.summary: This is a daily-life practice, not a sit. Several times a day, while walking, waiting or eating, let attention rest for a few breaths at the space just above the crown of the head, the "end of twelve", then carry on with what you were doing. Keep the touch light and brief. The remembering is the practice.
practices.sourceLabel: Vijñāna Bhairava verse 51 (the end-of-twelve, dvādaśānta, "however and wherever" through the day), tr. Christopher Hareesh Wallis (Tantra 112 full text) and his blog post on verses 49-51. The pack read "the twelve" as twelve body centres; the verse names one place, the end-of-twelve. Satsang summary in its own words.

practices.name: Merging the sense spaces (VBT verses 32-33)
cautions: If you feel disoriented, unreal or anxious, open the eyes, feel the feet and the seat, and stop for today.
The rest of the Vijñāna Bhairava (breath retention, mantra, the subtle-body and burning practices) is learned from a qualified teacher in the Trika tradition; Satsang lists places to practise.
practices.summary: Sit and bring attention to one sense contact: a sound, a touch, something seen. Notice the outer space where it arrives, the room and the distance. Then notice the inner space where it is received. Rest in both at once, the outer and the inner as one field with the sensation in the middle. When attention falls to one side, come back to both.
practices.sourceLabel: Vijñāna Bhairava verses 32-33 (merging the sensual spaces), tr. Christopher Hareesh Wallis (Tantra 112 full text) and his blog post on these verses. Satsang summary in its own words.

practices.name: Recollection of former lives (pubbenivāsānussati): orientation
cautions: No results are promised. Memories that seem to surface in meditation can be imagination or old impressions; the tradition warns against clinging to them either way.
Not for anyone living with dissociation, psychosis or unresolved trauma: stay with grounding breath practice and speak to a qualified teacher or clinician.
Do not try regression techniques from a summary or a video.

practices.sourceLabel: MN 4 (dhammatalks.org); Visuddhimagga XIII, tr. Ñāṇamoli, The Path of Purification (Access to Insight). Satsang summary in its own words.

ajahn-anan.name: Ajahn Anan
ajahn-anan.bio: Thai monk who ordained under Ajahn Chah in 1975 and founded Wat Marp Jan in Rayong; teaches weekly in Thai with English translation.

ajahn-brahm.name: Ajahn Brahm
ajahn-brahm.bio: British-born monk trained under Ajahn Chah in Thailand, abbot of Bodhinyana Monastery and spiritual director of the Buddhist Society of Western Australia.

ajahn-brahmali.name: Ajahn Brahmali
ajahn-brahmali.bio: Norwegian-born monk trained under Ajahn Brahm at Bodhinyana; teaches the early suttas and Vinaya closely, often co-teaching sutta courses with Bhante Sujato.

ajahn-nyanamoli.name: Ajahn Nyanamoli Thero
ajahn-nyanamoli.bio: Founder of Hillside Hermitage; ordained in the Thai Theravāda tradition and a monk since 2005, teaching from the early suttas.

ajahn-pasanno.name: Ajahn Pasanno
ajahn-pasanno.bio: Canadian monk who trained with Ajahn Chah, served as abbot of Wat Pah Nanachat and then co-abbot of Abhayagiri Buddhist Monastery.

ajahn-sona.name: Ajahn Sona
ajahn-sona.bio: Canadian monk and co-founder of Birken Forest Monastery in British Columbia, in the Thai forest tradition; known for practical talks on jhāna and daily life.

ajahn-sumedho.name: Ajahn Sumedho
ajahn-sumedho.bio: American-born senior Western disciple of Ajahn Chah who founded Chithurst and Amaravati monasteries in England and led them for decades.

alan-wallace.name: B. Alan Wallace
alan-wallace.bio: American scholar-practitioner ordained by the Dalai Lama and trained by Geshe Rabten, later a Stanford PhD, who teaches shamatha and Dzogchen and argues for a "contemplative science" of mind.

alexis-sanderson.name: Alexis Sanderson
alexis-sanderson.bio: Oxford Indologist of Shaiva tantra who read texts with Lakshmanjoo.

anandamayi-ma.name: Anandamayi Ma
anandamayi-ma.bio: Bengali saint, born Nirmala Sundari in present-day Bangladesh, whose spontaneous states of absorption drew devotees across India for six decades; she taught that all is God and that turning towards God is the one duty.

angela-puca.name: Angela Puca
angela-puca.bio: Scholar of Western esotericism and magic who runs Angela's Symposium, an academic channel on theurgy, Hermetic magic and the grimoire tradition.

bettina-baumer.name: Bettina Sharada Bäumer
bettina-baumer.bio: Austrian-born Indologist living in Varanasi; a student of Swami Lakshmanjoo who lectures on the Vijñāna Bhairava, Śiva Sūtras, Spanda and Netra Tantra and on Abhinavagupta's aesthetics.

brad-warner.name: Brad Warner
brad-warner.bio: American Sōtō Zen priest, author and former punk bassist who received transmission from Gudō Nishijima.

brother-chidananda.name: Brother Chidananda
brother-chidananda.bio: President and spiritual head of Self-Realization Fellowship / Yogoda Satsanga Society of India since 2017, teaching Yogananda's Kriya Yoga path.

charles-jones.name: Charles B. Jones
charles-jones.bio: Scholar of Chinese Pure Land and Taiwanese Buddhism at the Catholic University of America, author of Pure Land: History, Tradition, and Practice.

christopher-wallis.name: Christopher Wallis (Hareesh)
christopher-wallis.bio: Sanskrit scholar and practitioner of classical Śaiva Tantra who translates and teaches the non-dual texts of Kashmir Shaivism for modern practice.

cynthia-bourgeault.name: Cynthia Bourgeault
cynthia-bourgeault.bio: Episcopal priest and teacher of Centering Prayer and Wisdom Christianity who draws openly on Gurdjieff's Work.

dalai-lama.name: The 14th Dalai Lama
dalai-lama.bio: Tenzin Gyatso, the 14th Dalai Lama, a Gelug monk and scholar who has taught compassion and secular ethics worldwide from exile in Dharamsala.

daniel-matt.name: Daniel C. Matt
daniel-matt.bio: Scholar of Kabbalah and translator of the Pritzker Edition of the Zohar; studied under Alexander Altmann at Brandeis.

eric-steinhart.name: Eric Steinhart
eric-steinhart.bio: Philosophy professor whose short lectures explain Plotinus' One, emanation and the soul's fall and return.

father-spyridon.name: Father Spyridon
father-spyridon.bio: Orthodox priest who teaches the Jesus Prayer, repentance and the ascetic teaching of the Fathers in short talks.

filip-holm.name: Filip Holm
filip-holm.bio: Swedish scholar of religion and educator who runs Let's Talk Religion, long-form videos on mysticism across traditions.

francis-lucille.name: Francis Lucille
francis-lucille.bio: French-born non-dual teacher in the line of Jean Klein, known for dialogues that test every claim against direct experience.

goenka.name: S. N. Goenka
goenka.bio: Burmese-Indian lay teacher in the lineage of U Ba Khin whose ten-day vipassanā courses spread worldwide.

guo-gu.name: Guo Gu
guo-gu.bio: Guo Gu (Jimmy Yu), Dharma heir of Master Sheng Yen and professor of religion at Florida State University, who teaches silent illumination and huatou at the Tallahassee Chan Center.

henry-shukman.name: Henry Shukman
henry-shukman.bio: British poet and novelist who became a Sanbō Zen teacher and guiding teacher of Mountain Cloud Zen Center in Santa Fe.

jack-kornfield.name: Jack Kornfield
jack-kornfield.bio: American teacher who trained as a monk under Ajahn Chah and Mahasi Sayadaw, co-founded the Insight Meditation Society and Spirit Rock.

james-mallinson.name: James Mallinson
james-mallinson.bio: Boden Professor of Sanskrit at Oxford and leader of the Haṭha Yoga Project; edited the Khecarīvidyā, Dattātreyayogaśāstra and Amṛtasiddhi; also an initiated Rāmānandī mahant.

jiddu-krishnamurti.name: Jiddu Krishnamurti
jiddu-krishnamurti.bio: Indian speaker raised by the Theosophical Society, who left it in 1929 to teach that truth is a pathless land; much archive footage survives.

joan-halifax.name: Joan Halifax
joan-halifax.bio: American Zen teacher, anthropologist and founding abbot of Upaya Zen Center, known for her work on care for the dying.

justin-sledge.name: Justin Sledge
justin-sledge.bio: Historian of philosophy and religion who presents ESOTERICA, a channel on the history of mysticism, Gnosticism and Hermeticism.

kokyo-henkel.name: Kokyo Henkel
kokyo-henkel.bio: Soto Zen priest from the San Francisco Zen Center lineage, guiding teacher of Santa Cruz Zen Center, with a strong interest in buddha-nature texts.

lama-jampa-thaye.name: Lama Jampa Thaye
lama-jampa-thaye.bio: British-born lama authorised in the Sakya and Karma Kagyu traditions by Karma Thinley Rinpoche, founder of the Dechen community and a scholar of Tibetan Buddhism.

lama-yeshe.name: Lama Thubten Yeshe
lama-yeshe.bio: Tibetan lama who with Lama Zopa founded Kopan and the FPMT network.

laurence-freeman.name: Laurence Freeman OSB
laurence-freeman.bio: Benedictine monk, student and successor of John Main, and director of the World Community for Christian Meditation.

mark-dyczkowski.name: Mark Dyczkowski
mark-dyczkowski.bio: English Indologist and sitarist who lived four decades in Varanasi; initiated by Lakshmanjoo in 1976; translator of the Spanda texts, the Manthānabhairava Tantra and the 11-volume Tantrāloka. Died in Varanasi on 2 February 2025. Since April 2026 his students Arjun Seernels and Brian Campbell lead the Anuttara Trika Kula Reading Circles.

mingyur-rinpoche.name: Yongey Mingyur Rinpoche
mingyur-rinpoche.bio: Tibetan Kagyu and Nyingma teacher who founded Tergar, known for pairing meditation instruction with neuroscience and for a years-long wandering retreat.

nisargadatta-maharaj.name: Nisargadatta Maharaj
nisargadatta-maharaj.bio: Bombay teacher of the Inchegeri line whose dialogues in I Am That made 'I am' the doorway to the Absolute.

omid-safi.name: Omid Safi
omid-safi.bio: Duke University scholar of Islam who teaches Rumi, radical love and Sufi practice through his own courses and talks.

pema-chodron.name: Pema Chödrön
pema-chodron.bio: American nun and author, a student of Chögyam Trungpa, resident teacher at Gampo Abbey.

pierre-grimes.name: Pierre Grimes
pierre-grimes.bio: Platonist philosopher and founder of the Noetic Society, who read Plato, Plotinus and Proclus as a living practice he called philosophical midwifery.

pir-zia-inayat-khan.name: Pir Zia Inayat Khan
pir-zia-inayat-khan.bio: Head of the Inayatiyya since 2004, grandson of Hazrat Inayat Khan and founder of Suluk Academy; PhD in religion from Duke.

ringu-tulku.name: Ringu Tulku Rinpoche
ringu-tulku.bio: Karma Kagyu lama and scholar of the Rimé movement, former professor of Tibetan studies in Sikkim, who founded Bodhicharya and teaches in a light, accessible style.

robert-thurman.name: Robert A. F. Thurman
robert-thurman.bio: American scholar and translator, the first Westerner ordained a Tibetan Buddhist monk, Jey Tsong Khapa Professor at Columbia and co-founder of Tibet House US; died in June 2026.

rupert-spira.name: Rupert Spira
rupert-spira.bio: English potter turned teacher of the direct path, who points to awareness as the one reality behind all experience; a student of Francis Lucille.

sayadaw-u-tejaniya.name: Sayadaw U Tejaniya
sayadaw-u-tejaniya.bio: Burmese teacher known for a gentle 'awareness of the mind' style of insight practice.

sharon-salzberg.name: Sharon Salzberg
sharon-salzberg.bio: American teacher and co-founder of the Insight Meditation Society, best known for bringing mettā (lovingkindness) practice to the West.

sheng-yen.name: Master Sheng Yen
sheng-yen.bio: Taiwanese Chan master of the Linji and Caodong lines and founder of Dharma Drum Mountain, who revived Chan practice and taught in the West; his Great Dharma Drum TV series answers short questions.

swami-chinmayananda.name: Swami Chinmayananda
swami-chinmayananda.bio: Vedanta teacher who founded Chinmaya Mission and taught Swami Dayananda.

swami-dayananda-saraswati.name: Swami Dayananda Saraswati
swami-dayananda-saraswati.bio: Teacher of traditional Advaita Vedanta who founded the Arsha Vidya Gurukulams and trained Swami Tadatmananda among many others.

swami-lakshmanjoo.name: Swami Lakshmanjoo
swami-lakshmanjoo.bio: Kashmiri master regarded as the last living holder of the oral tradition of Kashmir Shaivism; his recorded teachings are kept by the Lakshmanjoo Academy.

swami-sarvadevananda.name: Swami Sarvadevananda
swami-sarvadevananda.bio: Monk of the Ramakrishna Order and minister of the Vedanta Society of Southern California in Hollywood.

swami-sarvapriyananda.name: Swami Sarvapriyananda
swami-sarvapriyananda.bio: Monk of the Ramakrishna Order and head of the Vedanta Society of New York, known for clear lectures on Advaita Vedanta and consciousness.

swami-tadatmananda.name: Swami Tadatmananda
swami-tadatmananda.bio: American-born monk and teacher of Advaita Vedanta and meditation at the Arsha Bodha Center in New Jersey, a disciple of Swami Dayananda Saraswati.

swami-tejomayananda.name: Swami Tejomayananda
swami-tejomayananda.bio: Disciple of Swami Chinmayananda and former head of the Chinmaya Mission worldwide.

swami-tyagananda.name: Swami Tyagananda
swami-tyagananda.bio: Monk of the Ramakrishna Order, head of the Ramakrishna Vedanta Society of Boston and Hindu chaplain at Harvard and MIT.

tara-brach.name: Tara Brach
tara-brach.bio: American psychologist and Insight meditation teacher who founded the Insight Meditation Community of Washington.

tenzin-wangyal.name: Tenzin Wangyal Rinpoche
tenzin-wangyal.bio: Bön lama trained at Menri under Lopön Tenzin Namdak, founder of Ligmincha International, who teaches Bön Dzogchen, dream yoga and the healing practices of sound and breath.

thanissaro-bhikkhu.name: Thanissaro Bhikkhu
thanissaro-bhikkhu.bio: American monk of the Thai forest Kammaṭṭhāna tradition, abbot of Metta Forest Monastery and a prolific translator of the Pāli suttas.

theodore-nottingham.name: Theodore Nottingham
theodore-nottingham.bio: Author and teacher who presents Gurdjieff's Fourth Way alongside the Christian contemplative tradition on his own channel.

thich-nhat-hanh.name: Thich Nhat Hanh
thich-nhat-hanh.bio: Vietnamese Zen monk, poet and peace activist who founded the Plum Village tradition and taught mindfulness and interbeing worldwide.

tom-cheetham.name: Tom Cheetham
tom-cheetham.bio: Philosopher and poet, the leading English-language interpreter of Henry Corbin and of the imaginal in Corbin and Hillman.

tsoknyi-rinpoche.name: Tsoknyi Rinpoche
tsoknyi-rinpoche.bio: Tibetan Drukpa Kagyu and Nyingma teacher, son of Tulku Urgyen Rinpoche, whose teaching on essence love and the subtle body works with modern stress.

tsultrim-allione.name: Lama Tsultrim Allione
tsultrim-allione.bio: American teacher, one of the first Western women ordained in Tibetan Buddhism (1970), founder of Tara Mandala and author of Women of Wisdom and Feeding Your Demons, a modern adaptation of Chöd.

william-chittick.name: William C. Chittick
william-chittick.bio: Scholar and translator of Ibn Arabi and Rumi; doctorate at Tehran University under Seyyed Hossein Nasr (1974).
